title: Light, shadows and the sky's calendar
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NCERT Class 4 'Our Sky' (Sun, Moon and stars; festivals and practices linked to the sky; shadows at different times of day and why their length changes) and Cambridge Primary Science Stage 4, Unit 5.4 'Light in the solar system' (the Sun as the light source; planets, moons, asteroids and comets). No textbook needed.
summary: Apart from the stars, everything we see in space shines with sunlight. Your child measures how shadows change with the Sun's height, finds the north-south line from the shortest shadow, makes an eclipse with a lamp and a bead, and keeps a month-long Moon diary. They learn how the Sun and the Moon set India's calendars and festivals. They meet comets, asteroids, the moons of other planets, Chandrayaan-3, and a woman who did the sums that predicted the return of Halley's comet.
builds_on: In Class 3 your child learned that the Sun is a star, the planets and the Moon reflect its light, and the Moon's phases come from how much of its lit half we see. In Class 2 (Day, night and rhythms of nature) they tracked a shadow stick. Next, in Class 5, they will use latitude and longitude, explain time zones and compare natural and artificial satellites.
goals: By the end your child can explain that the Sun lights the whole solar system, and that we see the Moon and planets by reflected sunlight.
By the end your child can measure shadows, explain why they are longest when the Sun is low, and use the shortest shadow to find north.
By the end your child can show with a model how solar and lunar eclipses are made by shadows in space.
By the end your child can keep a Moon diary and describe the pattern of phases across a month.
By the end your child can give examples of festivals and calendars set by the Sun and by the Moon.
By the end your child can describe asteroids, comets and moons, and say why a comet's tail points away from the Sun.

days.title: The sky all day long
days.goal: Recall Class 3 and start a month of sky-watching.

steps.title: What lights the sky?
steps.do: Recall Class 3. Ask: 'Which things in the sky make their own light? Which only reflect it? Why does the Moon change shape?' Good answers: 'The Sun and the stars make light. The Moon and the planets reflect it.' 'We see different amounts of the Moon's sunlit half.' Say: 'This year we follow sunlight: what it lights up, and where its shadows fall.'

steps.title: Sky from morning to night
steps.do: Ask your child to describe the sky at dawn, at midday, at sunset and at midnight: the colours, how bright it is, and what animals and people are doing. Make a quick drawing in four boxes. Ask: 'What changes? What causes every one of these changes?' (Where the Sun is.)

steps.title: Start the Moon diary
steps.do: Start Activity a1, the Moon diary. Today, look up the Moon's phase in a panchang or calendar. If the Moon is up tonight, look from a window, balcony or terrace. Draw it, and write the date, the time and where in the sky it was (east, high, west). Set a daily reminder for the next 30 days.

steps.title: Story: The Pigeon Who Watched for the Moon
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Stop when everyone on the roof is looking in the wrong direction and ask: 'Where would you look for a new crescent Moon, and why?' Finish the story and ask the story questions.

steps.title: Make a prediction
steps.do: Ask: 'Will the Moon rise at the same time every night? Why do you think so?' Write the guess inside the diary cover. You will check it on Day 5.

need: a notebook for the Moon diary
a calendar or panchang that shows Purnima and Amavasya

days.title: One lamp for the whole solar system
days.goal: See that the Moon and planets shine only by sunlight.

steps.title: Moon diary
steps.do: If the Moon was up, check last night's drawing. Ask: 'Where was it? What shape?'

steps.title: Sunlit worlds
steps.do: Do Experiment e1: a lamp, a white ball and a dark ball show how planets and moons are lit, and why one side is always dark.

steps.title: Earthshine
steps.do: Say: 'Look at a thin crescent Moon a few days after Amavasya. You can often see the rest of the Moon glowing faintly. That is earthshine: sunlight bounces off the Earth onto the Moon, then back to us. Leonardo da Vinci explained it in his notebook about 500 years ago.' Ask: 'So the Earth shines too. What would the Earth look like from the Moon?' (A big bright ball, with phases.)

steps.title: Draw the rays
steps.do: On a sheet, draw the Sun on the left, the Moon in the middle and an eye on the right. Your child uses a ruler to draw straight rays, with arrows, from the Sun to the Moon and from the Moon to the eye. Ask: 'Why is it a straight line?' (Light travels in straight lines.) Then ask: 'We can see Venus. Why can't we see a planet going round another star?' (It is very far away and reflects only a little light, so it is lost in its star's glare.)

steps.title: One sentence
steps.do: Your child finishes the sentence: 'The Moon and the planets I see at night are lit by ____.' (the Sun)

need: a lamp with the shade taken off
a white ball and a dark ball

days.title: Shadows: high Sun, low Sun
days.goal: Measure how a shadow's length changes with the height of the light.

steps.title: Moon diary and a guess
steps.do: Check the diary. Then ask: 'When is your shadow longest: in the morning, at noon or in the evening? Why do you think so?' Today's test will check the guess.

steps.title: Torch height and shadow length
steps.do: Do Experiment e2 with a torch, a crayon standing in clay and a ruler. Your child fills in the table and draws a bar chart.

steps.title: Why do shadows have sharp edges?
steps.do: Shine a torch past a pencil onto a wall. Ask: 'Why is the shadow the same shape as the pencil?' Good answer: 'Light goes in straight lines. It can't bend round the pencil.' Now hold the pencil near a tube light or a bright window. Ask: 'Why is this shadow fuzzy?' (A big light shines from many places at once.)

steps.title: Predict the real Sun
steps.do: Ask: 'Using your chart, when in the day will your shadow be longest? When will it be shortest?' Then measure your child's shadow with a measuring tape on a sunny balcony, terrace or the building compound, at about 9 am, 12 noon and 4 pm today. Write each length down.

need: a crayon and some clay or atta dough

days.title: The shadow that points north
days.goal: Use the shortest shadow of the day to find north and noon.

steps.title: The noon line
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Set up the stick at 11 am. Then go back every 15 minutes until 1:30 pm to mark the tip of the shadow.

steps.title: Jai Singh's giant sundials
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v1, Sawai Jai Singh II and the Jantar Mantar. Show a photo of the Samrat Yantra if you can. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Zero Shadow Day
steps.do: Say: 'In the part of India south of the Tropic of Cancer (Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Mumbai, Bhopal), the noon Sun is straight overhead on two days a year. For a moment, an upright pole has no shadow. In Bengaluru this happens around 24 April and 18 August.' Look up your city's dates and put them on the family calendar. Ask: 'Why can't Delhi or Srinagar ever have a Zero Shadow Day?' (They are north of the Tropic, so the Sun is never overhead there.)

steps.title: Check the noon line
steps.do: Look at the a2 marks. The shortest shadow shows local noon. Ask: 'What time did the clock say? Was it exactly 12?' Usually not. The whole of India uses one clock time, set for a line near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh. Local noon comes at about 12:10 in Chennai, 12:25 in Kochi, 12:40 in Mumbai and 11:35 in Kolkata, give or take a quarter of an hour with the season. Mark N on the line, then find east, south and west.

steps.title: Sun-path circle dance
steps.do: Stand on the noon line. Your child faces south and slowly draws the Sun's path with both arms: rising in the east on their left, highest at noon, sinking in the west on their right. Then they crouch and stretch their arms along the ground the opposite way, to show where the shadow points at each moment.

need: a straight stick or ruler, about 30 cm long
a lump of clay, or a heavy bottle and tape
a flat spot that gets sun from 11 am to 1:30 pm
chalk, or small pieces of paper and tape

days.title: Shadows in space: eclipses
days.goal: Make solar and lunar eclipses with a lamp, a ball and a bead.

steps.title: Moon diary check
steps.do: Look at the diary. Ask: 'Did the Moon rise at the same time each night?' (No. It rises about 50 minutes later each day.) Compare with the guess from Day 1.

steps.title: Make an eclipse
steps.do: Do Experiment e3 in a dark room. Your child holds the bead (Moon) and you hold the football (Earth). Make a solar eclipse, then a lunar eclipse, then a near miss, and ask each time: whose shadow is falling on whom?

steps.title: Aryabhata and the shadows
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v2, Aryabhata, who explained eclipses as shadows. Talk gently about the old story of Rahu swallowing the Sun: 'People everywhere made up stories for things they could not yet explain. Aryabhata looked at where the shadows fall and found the reason.' Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Wang Zhenyi's garden eclipse
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v4, Wang Zhenyi, who explained lunar eclipses in China over 200 years ago. The story told about her is that she made one with a round table, a hanging lamp and a mirror, just as you did with the football and the bead. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Safe eclipse watching
steps.do: Say: 'Never look at the Sun, even during an eclipse when most of it is covered. It can burn your eye without any pain. Use a pinhole instead.' Make a pinhole in a card. On a sunny balcony, stand with your back to the Sun and hold the card so its shadow falls on white paper. The small bright circle inside the shadow is a picture of the Sun. Look only at the paper.

steps.title: Sort the eclipses
steps.do: Ask: 'In a solar eclipse, whose shadow falls on whom? In a lunar eclipse?' (The Moon's shadow falls on the Earth. The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.) Ask: 'Which phase must the Moon be in for each?' (New Moon for a solar eclipse, full Moon for a lunar eclipse.)

need: a small bead or marble on a stick (Moon)

days.title: The sky's calendar
days.goal: Learn how the Sun and the Moon set our calendars and festivals.

steps.title: Moon diary check
steps.do: Check the diary: is the Moon growing (Shukla Paksha) or shrinking (Krishna Paksha)? Is it seen in the evening or the early morning?

steps.title: Sun calendars and Moon calendars
steps.do: Say: 'A year is set by the Sun: one trip round it. A month is set by the Moon: about 29 and a half days from one Amavasya to the next. Twelve Moon months make only about 354 days. So a calendar that follows only the Moon slips about 11 days a year against the seasons.' Ask: 'Why does Eid come about 11 days earlier every year?' (The Islamic calendar follows only the Moon.) Ask: 'Why does Deepavali always come in October or November?' (Hindu calendars add an extra month, Adhik Maas, every two or three years, to keep step with the Sun.)

steps.title: Festival sort
steps.do: Do Activity a3. Your child sorts the twelve festival slips into Sun and Moon piles, then finds the Purnima and Amavasya festivals. Ask: 'Which ones stay on nearly the same date every year?'

steps.title: The nakshatras
steps.do: Say: 'Indian sky-watchers divided the Moon's path into 27 star groups, the nakshatras. The Moon spends about one day in each. Rohini, Krittika and Chitra are nakshatras, and many people are named after them.' If someone in the family knows their birth nakshatra, find out which it is. On a clear night, look for Krittika, also called the Pleiades: a tiny, misty group of stars.

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Your child does the core worksheet ws1. Read the questions aloud if needed, and let them use the noon line and Moon diary to help.

need: the festival cards from Activity a3

days.title: Comets, asteroids, moons and Chandrayaan
days.goal: Meet the smaller members of the Sun's family.

steps.title: Moon diary check
steps.do: Check the diary and add tonight's Moon. Ask: 'How many days since Amavasya? What shape do you expect in three days?'

steps.title: Rocks and snowballs
steps.do: Say: 'Between Mars and Jupiter is a belt of millions of rocky lumps, the asteroids. Far beyond Neptune there are icy ones. A comet is a ball of ice and dust. When it comes near the Sun, some ice turns to gas. Sunlight and the solar wind, a stream of tiny particles from the Sun, push the gas and dust out into a glowing tail. So the tail always points away from the Sun.' Ask: 'When a comet is moving away from the Sun, which goes first, the head or the tail?' (The tail, because it still points away from the Sun.)

steps.title: The woman who timed a comet
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v3, Nicole-Reine Lepaute and the return of Halley's comet. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Chandrayaan-3
steps.do: Say: 'On 23 August 2023, India's Chandrayaan-3 lander, Vikram, landed near the Moon's south pole. No spacecraft had landed so close to it before. The small rover Pragyan rolled out and studied the soil, and found sulphur. Scientists are interested in the south pole because some of its craters never get sunlight and may hold ice.' Ask: 'Why would a crater never get sunlight?' (Near the pole the Sun stays low, so the floors of deep craters stay in shadow.)

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Your child does the stretch worksheet ws2. Ask them to explain the comet-tail question aloud before writing.

need: pictures of Halley's comet and Chandrayaan-3 if you can find them

days.title: Race to the Moon, check and teach it back
days.goal: Bring the light and shadows together and teach it back.

steps.title: Race to the Moon
steps.do: Play the board game g1. Players must answer a question on every 'sky square' they land on.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Your child tries the challenge worksheet ws3. Talk through the eclipse puzzle with the lamp and bead if needed.

steps.title: End check
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud. Return to the lamp for any muddle.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches a family member, using the lamp, the ball and the bead: 'The Sun lights the Moon and the planets. Shadows are long when the Sun is low. An eclipse is a shadow in space. The Moon's phases make our months.' Then they show the Moon diary so far and predict tonight's shape. Keep the diary going to finish the month for the project.

need: the game board, die and counters

the Moon is too small to make a shadow

a ball of ice and dust that grows a tail near the Sun

Kavya in Chennai watches a lunar eclipse at night. Her cousin Farhan in Dubai, where it is also night, sees it at the same time. But a total solar eclipse can be seen only from a narrow strip of land. Why the difference?
On 21 March, at noon, Revathi stands a stick upright on the Equator. What does its shadow look like?
A thin crescent Moon is seen just after sunset. Which way does its bright curve face?
opts: away from where the Sun set

sections.p: Some families avoid cooking or eating during an eclipse. What test could you do to find out whether eclipse light changes food? What is the one real danger of an eclipse?

Two groups decide when Eid begins. Ayesha's group waits until someone has really seen the thin new Moon. Hafsa's group works out in advance, with calculations, when it can be seen. Pick one side and give a reason. Then say one good point of the other side.
Indian calendars add an extra month called Adhik ____ to keep step with the Sun.
Set by the Sun or by the Moon?

Alexis Clairaut published the sums that predicted the return of Halley's comet, and left out Nicole-Reine Lepaute's name. His helper Jérôme Lalande later wrote that the work could not have been done without her. If you were a historian today, what evidence would you look for to find out who did the work?

experiments.title: Sunlit worlds
experiments.question: Why does every planet and moon have a bright side and a dark side?
need: a lamp with the shade taken off (the Sun)
a white ball and a dark ball
steps: Put the lamp on a table in the middle of a dark room.
You hold the white ball about a metre from the lamp. Your child walks slowly in a circle round the ball, looking at it all the time.
Ask: 'Which side of the ball is bright? Which side is dark?'
Try the dark ball the same way. Ask: 'Which ball is easier to see?'
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will you ever see the ball bright all over? Why do you think so?'
experiments.observe: The side facing the lamp is always bright and the far side is always dark. From beside the ball you see half bright and half dark. The white ball is easier to see than the dark one.
experiments.why: Planets and moons make no light of their own. The Sun lights the half facing it, and that half has day. How bright a planet looks depends on how much sunlight reaches it and how much its surface reflects. Venus is wrapped in white clouds, so it looks very bright. The Moon is dark grey rock and reflects only about a tenth of the light that hits it. It looks bright to us because it is so close.

experiments.title: Torch height and shadow length
experiments.question: How does the height of the light change the length of a shadow?
need: a crayon, about 5 cm tall, standing in a lump of clay or atta dough
books to rest the torch on
steps: In a dim room, stand the crayon upright on a table.
Put the torch on the table, 30 cm from the crayon, shining at it. This is like the Sun at sunrise. Look: the shadow runs right off the table.
Now raise the torch on books, so the bulb is 10 cm, 15 cm, 20 cm, 30 cm and 40 cm above the table. Keep it 30 cm away and pointing at the crayon. Measure the shadow each time.
Write a table with two columns: how high the torch is, and how long the shadow is.
Draw a bar for each height.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'When the torch is higher, will the shadow be longer or shorter? Why do you think so?'
experiments.observe: With the torch on the table, the shadow is longer than the table. At 10 cm high it is about 30 cm long, at 15 cm about 15 cm, at 20 cm about 10 cm, and at 40 cm only about 4 cm. It shrinks fast at first, then slowly.
experiments.why: The crayon blocks straight rays of light. When the light comes in low, the rays skim past the top of the crayon and hit the table far away, so the shadow is long. When the light comes from high up, the rays hit the table close to the crayon. The real Sun is low at sunrise and sunset and highest around noon, so shadows are longest in the morning and evening.
experiments.safety: Don't shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

experiments.title: Make an eclipse
experiments.question: How do shadows in space make eclipses?
need: a small bead or marble on a stick (the Moon)
steps: Put the lamp on a table and the football 1–2 metres away.
Hold the bead between the lamp and the football, close to the football, until its shadow falls on it. Look at the small dark spot. People standing there would see a total solar eclipse.
Now move the bead to the far side of the football, into the football's shadow. The bead goes dark: a lunar eclipse.
Move the bead a little above or below the line. Ask: 'Does the shadow still fall on the other ball?'
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Which shadow will be bigger, the Moon's shadow on the Earth or the Earth's shadow on the Moon? Why?'
experiments.observe: The bead's shadow on the football is tiny. The football's shadow covers the whole bead. When the bead is a little above or below the line, there is no eclipse.
experiments.why: In a solar eclipse, the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth. Its shadow falls on a small patch of Earth, and only people there see the Sun covered. In a lunar eclipse, the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. Everyone on the night side can see the Moon go dark, often a coppery red, because a little sunlight bends through the Earth's air. The Moon's path is tilted slightly, so in most months the shadows miss and there is no eclipse.
experiments.safety: Never look at the real Sun during an eclipse. Don't touch the hot bulb.

activities.title: A month-long Moon diary
steps: Every evening, look for the Moon from a window, balcony or terrace. If it isn't up in the evening, look in the early morning.
Draw its shape, and write the date, the time and where it is (low east, high, low west).
From the calendar, write whether it is Shukla Paksha (growing) or Krishna Paksha (shrinking).
After a week, compare: is it rising later? Is it growing or shrinking?
After a month, cut out the drawings and arrange them in a circle.
activities.outcome: A real record of one full cycle of the Moon, showing the phases and the Moon rising about 50 minutes later each day.

activities.title: The noon line: find north from a shadow
need: a straight stick or ruler, about 30 cm long
a lump of clay, or a heavy bottle and tape
a flat spot on a terrace, balcony or compound that gets sun from 11 am to 1:30 pm
chalk, or small pieces of paper and tape
a thread with a small weight tied on
steps: At 11 am, stand the stick upright on the flat spot in the clay, or tape it to the bottle. Hang the weighted thread beside it to check it is straight up.
Every 15 minutes until about 1:30 pm, mark the tip of the shadow and write the time.
Find the shortest shadow. Draw a line from the foot of the stick through that mark. This is the noon line. It runs exactly north and south.
For most of the year, the shortest shadow points north. South of the Tropic of Cancer, between the two Zero Shadow Days (about May to July), it points south instead. Mark N, then E, S and W.
Write down the clock time of the shortest shadow.
activities.outcome: A north-south line found from the Sun alone, and the time of local noon at your home.

activities.title: Festival sort: set by the Sun or the Moon?
steps: Write one festival on each slip: Pongal, Vishu, Puthandu (Tamil New Year), Makar Sankranti, Baisakhi, Ugadi, Karthigai Deepam, Ganesh Chaturthi, Deepavali, Holi, Eid al-Fitr, Buddha Purnima.
With your help, your child sorts them into two piles: 'set by the Sun's position' and 'set by the Moon's phase'.

For each Moon festival, find out whether it falls on Purnima, on Amavasya or on a set day of a Paksha. (Karthigai Deepam, Holi and Buddha Purnima are on a full Moon. Deepavali is around Amavasya. Ugadi is the day after Amavasya. Ganesh Chaturthi is the fourth day of Shukla Paksha. Eid starts when the new crescent is seen.)
Ask: 'Which festivals fall on almost the same date every year? Why?' (The Sun festivals. Pongal and Makar Sankranti come around 14 January, and Vishu, Puthandu and Baisakhi around 14 April.)
activities.outcome: A sorted set of festival slips and an understanding that our calendars come from the sky.

project.title: The Moon month poster
steps: Keep the Moon diary (Activity a1) every day for a whole month.
At the end, cut out each night's drawing.
Arrange them in a circle round a picture of the Earth, with the Sun drawn on one side.
Mark Amavasya, Purnima, Shukla Paksha and Krishna Paksha.
Add the festivals that fell during your month.
project.outcome: A poster of one real Moon month from your child's own observations, showing how the Moon and our festivals are linked.

game.title: Race to the Moon
rules: Start on EARTH. Roll and move.
On a 'Sky question' square, another player asks a question from this week. A right answer moves you on 2.
Follow the instructions on the other squares.
The first to land exactly on THE MOON wins and must explain why the Moon shines.
squares: Long morning shadow: what time is it?
You looked at the Sun: back to start
Comet tail: which way does it point?
Lunar eclipse: name whose shadow it is
Jantar Mantar: what is it for?
Solar eclipse: use a pinhole, move on 1
Lost in a shadowed crater: miss a turn

big: If the Sun went out, how long would it take us to notice, and what would we still see?
Should calendars follow the Sun, the Moon or both? What do we gain and lose either way?
Who should get the credit for a discovery made by a team?
Some craters on the Moon may hold ice. Who should be allowed to use it: whoever gets there first, or everyone?

challenge.q: 'The far side of the Moon is the dark side.' Is it?
challenge.hint: The Moon always shows us the same face, so the far side is hidden from us. It is not dark. It gets just as much sunlight, and at new Moon, when our side is dark, the far side is fully lit. What would be a better name for it?

challenge.q: 'The Moon is bigger when it is rising.' Is it?
challenge.hint: Hold a coin at arm's length and see how much of the rising Moon it covers. Check again when the Moon is high. It covers the same amount. This 'Moon illusion' happens in our brains, and scientists still argue about exactly why.

challenge.q: 'Eclipses are harmful to food and people.' Are they?
challenge.hint: There is no evidence that eclipse light changes food or harms anyone, indoors or outdoors. The one real danger is looking at the Sun, which can burn the eye. Many families keep eclipse customs out of respect and tradition. That is a different question from what is harmful.

perspectives.view: Many Muslim communities begin Eid only when someone has really seen the new crescent. Others use calculations to decide in advance. Both groups know the science. Ask: why might some people prefer to see it for themselves, even when calculation is possible?

On some coral reefs, such as Australia's Great Barrier Reef, many corals release their eggs together a few nights after a full Moon in late spring. They have no eyes but they sense moonlight. Ask: what other living things might keep a Moon calendar?
Pigeons can find their way home using the position of the Sun together with their own body clock. Ask: what would happen to a pigeon's sun compass if their body clock were wrong?

voices.who: Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II (1688–1743), Jaipur, India
voices.idea: He built five observatories, the Jantar Mantars, in Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura in the early 1700s. Their giant stone instruments, like the Samrat Yantra in Jaipur, the world's largest sundial, measure time and the positions of the Sun and stars by shadows.
voices.then: He built big because big instruments give finer readings: the shadow of the Samrat Yantra moves about 6 centimetres a minute, so time can be read to about 2 seconds. Telescopes were already in use in Europe, and later critics said his stone instruments were out of date.
voices.now: The Jaipur Jantar Mantar is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and still tells accurate local time. Historians agree the instruments are very precise for naked-eye astronomy, though telescopes soon did better.
voices.ask: Jai Singh chose very big stone instruments over the new small telescopes. What are the good and bad points of each? Is newer always better?

voices.idea: In the Aryabhatiya (499 CE) he explained that a lunar eclipse happens when the Moon enters the Earth's shadow, and a solar eclipse when the Moon covers the Sun, and he worked out how to calculate them.
voices.then: Some later astronomers, including Brahmagupta, criticised parts of his work, and the popular story of the demon Rahu swallowing the Sun stayed alive for centuries.
voices.now: His explanation is the one scientists accept today. Eclipses can now be predicted to within seconds for centuries ahead.
voices.ask: Aryabhata could not fly into space to check. What clues on the ground could tell him that a lunar eclipse is the Earth's shadow? (Hint: what shape is the shadow's edge?)

voices.idea: Edmond Halley had predicted that a comet seen in 1682 would return around 1758. In 1757–1758, Lepaute worked for months with the mathematicians Alexis Clairaut and Jérôme Lalande, doing the huge hand calculations of how Jupiter's and Saturn's pull would delay it. They predicted it would come closest to the Sun in mid April 1759, within about a month either way.
voices.then: The comet came closest on 13 March 1759, within their margin. Clairaut published the work and left her name out. Lalande later praised her, saying the calculation could not have been done without her.
voices.now: Historians now give her a large share of the credit, and a crater on the Moon and an asteroid are named after her. The comet is named after Halley.
voices.ask: If you had done months of the sums and someone else's name went on the result, how would you feel? How can we find out who really did the work in the past?

voices.idea: In Qing-dynasty China, where few girls were taught science, she studied astronomy and mathematics from her grandfather's library. In an essay on lunar eclipses she explained them correctly as the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon. The story told of her is that she showed it with a round table as the Earth, a lamp hanging from the roof as the Sun and a mirror as the Moon. She wrote books to make mathematics easier for ordinary readers, and a poem asking whether daughters could not also be heroes.
voices.then: Women's scholarship was rarely published or honoured. She died at 29, and much of her work survived only because a friend kept her manuscripts.
voices.now: Her explanation of eclipses is the accepted one. A crater on Venus is named after her. Historians note that some details of the garden model come from later retellings.
voices.ask: Wang Zhenyi and Aryabhata, over a thousand years and thousands of kilometres apart, both explained eclipses as shadows. What does that tell you about whether science belongs to one country?

check.q: Why can we see the Moon and planets at night?
check.a: Sunlight reflects off them into our eyes.

check.q: Why is your shadow longest in the morning and evening?
check.a: The Sun is low, so its light comes in at a slant and the shadow stretches out far.

check.q: How can you find north using a stick and the Sun?
check.a: Mark the tip of a stick's shadow around midday. The shortest shadow lies on the north-south line. For most of the year in India it points north.

check.q: What is a solar eclipse? A lunar eclipse?
check.a: Solar: the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and its shadow falls on Earth. Lunar: the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

check.q: Does the Moon rise at the same time every night?
check.a: No. It rises about 50 minutes later each night, because the Moon moves along its orbit while the Earth spins.

check.q: Name one festival set by the Sun and one set by the Moon.
check.a: Sun: Pongal, Vishu, Puthandu, Makar Sankranti. Moon: Deepavali, Karthigai Deepam, Ugadi, Eid, Buddha Purnima.

check.q: Why does a comet's tail point away from the Sun?
check.a: Sunlight and the Sun's wind push the gas and dust away from the Sun.

story.title: The Pigeon Who Watched for the Moon
text: My name is Badshah, and I am a pigeon. Not a common pigeon of the station roof, you understand, but a pigeon of an old house near the Charminar in Hyderabad, where Zoya's grandfather has kept pigeons in a wooden loft on the roof for fifty years. Every evening he waves his long bamboo pole with the red cloth on the end, and we rise together into the sky, round and round, and come home when he whistles.

I know the sky better than any human. I know where the Sun is at every hour, because that is how I find my way. When I am taken far away in a basket and let go, I feel for the Sun, and I feel for the time in my own body, and from the two together I know which way home lies. The Sun is my compass. I never think about it. I just know.
But that evening, the humans were thinking only about the Moon.

It was the twenty-ninth day of Ramzan. All month the family had fasted from before dawn until sunset, and now everyone wanted to know one thing: would the new Moon be seen tonight? If it was, Eid would be tomorrow. If not, there would be one more day of fasting.

So at sunset, the whole roof filled with people. Zoya's grandfather in his white kurta. Her mother, with the youngest on her hip. Her cousins, pushing and pointing. And from the roof next door, separated only by a low wall, came Sravya, Zoya's best friend, and her grandmother, who climbed the stairs slowly with one hand on her knee. Sravya's family did not keep Ramzan, but they always came up for chand raat. "It is the same Moon," Sravya's grandmother said, "that tells me when Deepavali is."
Everyone stared at the sky. And everyone, I noticed, was staring the wrong way.

The cousins looked straight up, where the full Moon sails. Sravya looked east, where the big orange Moon of Purnima rises. Zoya's grandfather, whose eyes were not what they had been, looked everywhere at once. The sky darkened from gold to pink to violet. The azaan for maghrib rang out from the mosque. Still nobody saw anything, and their faces began to fall.

Zoya had been very quiet. For the last month she had been keeping a Moon diary for school, drawing the Moon every evening in a little notebook with a cover of blue paper. I had seen her up here every night, peering, scribbling, frowning. She had drawn the full Moon rising in the east like a lamp. She had drawn it getting thinner, night after night, coming up later and later until she had to get up before dawn to see it, a thin silver curve low in the east just before the Sun came up. And then for a day or two she had drawn nothing at all, because there was nothing to draw.

She opened the notebook now and looked at it for a long time. Then she looked at the place where the Sun had just gone down, behind the domes and minarets of the old city, where the sky was still glowing.

"The Moon is lit by the Sun," she said, to nobody in particular. "The bright side always faces the Sun. When it's new, it's right next to the Sun, so you can't see it at all. And the day after, it's moved a tiny bit away." She pointed. "So it has to be there. Low down. Just above where the Sun went. And the bright edge will be at the bottom, facing the Sun."
Sravya looked at her. Then she turned round. Then everyone turned round.
I flew up, because I wanted to see it first. I rose over the roofs of the old city, over the kites and the water tanks and the washing lines, and I looked west, into the last of the light.

And there it was, so thin it was hardly there at all. A silver eyelash of light, lying almost on its back just above the glow where the Sun had set, with its bright curve turned down towards the hidden Sun, exactly as Zoya had said.

"Chand!" shouted one of the cousins. "Chand dikh gaya!" And then everybody was shouting, and hugging, and Zoya's grandfather was saying a prayer, and from roofs all across the old city came cheers and the bang of crackers, and people were calling "Eid Mubarak!" over the walls.
Sravya's grandmother held Zoya's face in her hands and kissed her forehead. "Sharp eyes," she said.
"Not sharp eyes," said Zoya, a little embarrassed. "Just a diary."

I came down to the loft as the grandfather whistled. In a few minutes the thin Moon followed the Sun down behind the minarets, and was gone. The humans would sleep tonight and celebrate tomorrow, and Sravya and her grandmother would come to eat sheer khurma, as they did every year.

I settled on my perch. Humans are strange. They need notebooks to know what we pigeons feel in our bones: everything in the sky is tied to the Sun, and if you know where the Sun is, you know where to look for everything else. But Zoya found the Moon with a pencil, and I found it with wings, and we were looking at the same thin light.
story.epiphany: The Moon is lit by the Sun, so its bright side always faces the Sun. A new crescent sits close to the Sun in the sky, low in the west just after sunset, with its bright edge towards where the Sun went down. The turn comes when Zoya uses her Moon diary to work out where to look, while everyone else searches the wrong part of the sky. Two families with different festivals share one Moon, and a careful record finds what eager eyes miss.
ask: Why was everyone looking in the wrong place?
How did Zoya's Moon diary help her know where to look?
Why is the bright edge of the crescent turned towards where the Sun set?
Sravya's grandmother said it was the same Moon that tells her when Deepavali is. What did she mean?
Badshah finds his way using the Sun. Zoya finds the Moon using the Sun. What does that tell you about the Sun?

ideas.idea: One lamp lights the whole solar system.
ideas.more: Every planet, moon, asteroid and comet tail we see is lit by the Sun. Their phases, shadows and eclipses are all just the Sun's light being blocked or bounced.
A shadow's length tells you how high the Sun is. Its direction tells you north and the time. The round edge of the Earth's shadow on the Moon in an eclipse shows that the Earth is round.

ideas.idea: Our calendars and festivals are set by the Sun and the Moon.
ideas.more: The day comes from the Earth's spin, the month from the Moon, and the year from the trip round the Sun. People all over India still time their lives by them.

unknowns: How much ice is hidden in the Moon's dark polar craters, and how did it get there? Missions including India's Chandrayaan-1 found signs of water, but nobody yet knows how much there is.
Why does the rising Moon look bigger? Scientists have argued about the Moon illusion for over 2,000 years and still don't fully agree.
Where did the Earth's water come from? Some may have come from comets or asteroids, and some may have been here from the start. Scientists are still arguing.
